solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Awful toothache swallowing most of cold drink (3,9)

indicators.note: an awful version of the word is a badly mangled one
the jumbled letters take the other piece inside them
all but the last letter is kept

blocks.note: anagram fodder, jumbled around the next piece

explanation.surface: Someone with raging toothache is struggling to sip a cold drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Cold drinks are exactly what hurt a bad tooth, which is why 'cold drink' reads as one phrase; in fact 'cold' feeds the wordplay and the answer is a hot drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: cocoa stirred into hot milk is one particular drink among many.

indicators.note: a gruesome version of the word is a grotesquely twisted one

explanation.surface: A tough, gruesome monster out of a horror story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like an adjective describing the monster, or even the novelist Thomas Hardy, but it is only letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hydra is the many-headed monster of Greek myth.

indicators.note: a variety of the word is another arrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: A kind of fruit grown in Argentina.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Variety' belongs naturally to fruit, so the clue reads as a plain description of a South American crop.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangerine is a small orange citrus fruit.

clue.text: Bay and hazel, perhaps, on either side of box tree (5,8)

indicators.note: the first two pieces sit at the two ends with the third between

blocks.note: a bay is a reddish-brown horse
the hazel bears a nut, the hazelnut; 'perhaps' marks it as one example

explanation.surface: Bay and hazel planted on each side of a box tree, as in a garden hedge.
explanation.walkthrough: Bay, hazel and box are all shrubs, so the clue looks like planting notes; each has to be read in another sense, and 'tree' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The horse chestnut is a large tree that bears conkers.

indicators.note: in a down clue the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An antiques collector makes the highest bid for an old chest at auction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top bid' reads as the winning bid at an auction; 'top' actually belongs to 'Collector's' and takes its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words name a strong box for keeping money or valuables.

clue.text: Finger broken after headcase forms group of extremists (7,6)

indicators.note: a broken word has its letters rearranged
this piece comes after the next one

explanation.surface: A broken finger turns a madman into the leader of a gang of fanatics.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is built back to front: the anagram is written first but reads second in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The lunatic fringe is the most extreme minority within a movement.

indicators.note: the letter named is taken out

blocks.note: a teal is a small duck

explanation.surface: Duck was left off the menu for the meal.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain tea can be an evening meal, not just a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea is a light afternoon or early evening meal in Britain.

clue.text: In favour of not running quickly (6)

indicators.note: letters that are running have been set in motion into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone who prefers not to rush anywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface prefers walking to running, then the answer means the opposite: fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrowed from Italian and Spanish, this is informal English for doing something at once, fast.

indicators.note: the first piece goes inside the second

explanation.surface: A benefactor's name carved above a building's entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: Donors' names really are carved over doorways, so the picture fits the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe a person who gives money or help to a cause.

indicators.note: one piece is placed up against the other

blocks.note: F = fine, as on pencil leads

explanation.surface: Someone biased against a lovely amusement park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prejudiced against' reads as one phrase; 'against' is really the joining instruction, putting UNFAIR beside F.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in British usage, where a travelling fair of rides and stalls counts as an amusement park.

indicators.note: the named letter is not there

explanation.surface: A monkey wrapped in a cloak because it isn't cold.
explanation.walkthrough: C for cold is the tap label.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: gorillas, chimps and orang-utans all belong to the primate order.

clue.text: Problem caused by too much reading, of course, in English school (9)

definitions.text: Problem caused by too much reading

indicators.note: the piece goes in the middle of the others

explanation.surface: An English school where pupils read so much it causes problems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' is the verb, to train, not a place; 'of course' is the everyday agreement, yes.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyestrain is the tiredness of the eyes that long reading brings on.

clue.text: Creature in a stream grabbing frantic duck (9)

indicators.note: the stream holds the next piece inside it

blocks.note: a rill is a small stream
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, O

explanation.surface: Something in a stream seizes a panicking duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like the stream's victim, but it is a cricket score of zero.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this armoured South American mammal is just one of countless creatures.

clue.text: Trust I placed in big hospital (5)

indicators.note: I is put inside the next word

blocks.note: H = hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A patient putting trust in a large hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big hospital' looks like one phrase but splits into FAT and H.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to have belief and confidence in someone is to trust them.

indicators.note: the article is taken inside the next word

blocks.note: THE is the definite article, inside FAR

explanation.surface: An antique acquired by a distant forebear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remote ancestor' reads as one phrase; 'remote' is the wordplay, and a father is an ancestor however close.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a parent is the nearest of all ancestors, so 'remote' belongs to the wordplay.

clue.text: Gem carved in relief arrived with ring (5)

explanation.surface: A carved gem arrives set in a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The ring looks like jewellery for the gem; it is just the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: A cameo is a gem carved in relief, the figure raised against the background.

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: a restaurant specialising in food cooked over direct heat

explanation.surface: Showing a restaurant that is near where you live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screen' looks like a verb, to screen a film or a candidate; it is the noun, a grating.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a grating of bars set over a window or opening screens what lies behind it.

clue.text: Bursar, more confident following adjustment of rate (9)

indicators.note: an adjustment rearranges the letters
this piece comes after the other

explanation.surface: A college bursar grows more confident after the interest rate is changed.
explanation.walkthrough: A bursar handles money, so an adjusted rate fits the picture exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a bursar keeps the accounts of a school or college, the financial officer's job.

clue.text: First man heading off for weir? (3)

indicators.note: the word's head, its first letter, comes off

blocks.note: Adam, the first man in Genesis, minus his first letter

explanation.surface: Adam wandering off to look at a weir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading off' reads as setting out; it means losing the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A dam, like a weir, is a barrier across a river.

indicators.note: the word turns over, running backwards

blocks.note: denim is a cotton material, here written backwards

explanation.surface: Someone digging up cloth that has come over from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dug up' is the definition, not a direction for the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Mined means extracted from the ground, dug up.

indicators.note: to re-sort letters is to sort them again into a new order

explanation.surface: A holiday home that is always available to rent near a seaside resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' reads as a seaside town; split as re-sort it is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternal means without end, continuous.

indicators.note: the answer lies in the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across novEL Fantasy

explanation.surface: A fairy appearing in a fantasy novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets are only surface dressing; the letters run straight across them.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: folklore uses both words for the same small magical beings.

indicators.note: the answer sits at the heart of the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across maNY LONdoners

explanation.surface: A fabric that many people in London cannot do without.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vital' suggests importance; here it means inside, at the vitals.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this synthetic fibre is one material among many, used for stockings and rope.

clue.text: Taken from album not intended for release? (3,3,6)

blocks.note: a track taken off a record

explanation.surface: A track lifted from an album that was never meant to be released.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is literal, a song off a record; the second is the journalist's phrase for a remark not to be published.
explanation.definitionFit: Off the record means said privately, not for publication.
